catalog_quote: There are some vowels in the data which are not included in Figure 7. The vowels [o ŏ] are probably allophones of /əu əŭ/, occurring in unstressed syllables or shortened by a glottal stop. There are a few cases where [a ă] likewise seem to be shortened forms of an open -> close diphthong, and [i] seems to be a shortened or unstressed pronunciation of /ei/ or /i/. ... Phonation, tone, and glottalization act in concert in Padaung, making it difficult to know a priori which of the features is contrastive. Padaung has three tones: high falling [42], mid [3], and low tones [2] and [1]. Tone [1] is always closed with a glottal stop in utterance final position. Tone [3] can optionally be closed with a glottal stop. Phonation can occur on the mid [3] and low tone which I have labelled [2]. Breathy vowels are not closed with a glottal stop.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Padaung (Kayan) is described as a tone language (3-4 tones interacting with phonation and final glottal stop); the only reference to stress is that reduced vowels [ɐ ə] occur in unstressed syllables (i.e. there are unstressed, reduced syllables alongside full tonal syllables). The source gives no rule for where word stress falls; by implication the pattern is the Karenic sesquisyllabic one (reduced toneless presyllable + full final syllable), which Manson 2009 states only as an areal generalisation ('sesquisyllabic (i.e. they have iambic stress)'), not for Kayan specifically.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Kauffman flags his Padaung tone/phonation analysis as untested ('I have not tested which of those features, if any, is contrastive').
new_statements.domain_note: Based on a 406-item wordlist elicited mostly in isolation (citation forms) from one speaker (Lapi, c. 40, farmer from Demoso, NW Kayah State) recorded in Thailand; a 5-page synchronic sketch inside a comparative-tonal MA thesis, not a full phonology. The authoritative descriptions (Manson 2007, 2010) were not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: All material located concerns the Pekon/Demoso 'Padaung' = Kayan Lahwi [pdu], kaya1315: Manson's 2007/2010 works describe the Pekon (Phekhon) dialect, the standard variety (Glottolog lgcode 'Pekon = Kayan [pdu]'); Kauffman 1993's 'Padaung' speaker is from Demoso, NW Kayah State; Luangthongkum's 'Kayan' is from Huai Suea Thao, Mae Hong Son (Padaung refugee community). Ywar 2013 (fetched sources) is Kayan Lahta (Lahta-Zayein cluster, zaye1235/kxk), a different, mutually unintelligible language, and must not be used for kaya1315. Shintani's many 'X Kayan' LSTCA doculects are village-named and their assignment to pdu vs. Yinbaw/Gekho/Lahta could not be verified.
